book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask
title: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask
answer: Every parent should be able to ask five questions about how their child's school uses AI: which tools touch a child's information, whether signed agreements cover those tools, who makes decisions about a child, how the school teaches children to use AI well, and what a parent can do with a concern. A school that answers these clearly shows it has done the work, and the answers build the trust that makes everything else possible.

sections.body: This idea gives families a simple way to check how their children's school handles AI. It sets out five questions parents should be able to ask, each paired with the kind of answer a good school gives. A school that cannot answer them clearly still has work to do, and board members can use the same questions to check on their district. The point is that parents have a right to understand how AI is used with their children, and clear answers turn that right into something real rather than something families have to guess at.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school that follows this idea, the first question is answered by a public list of approved tools that shows which ones a particular child uses. The second is answered by confirming that every tool handling student data is covered by a signed agreement limiting how that data is used. For the third, the school states that people, not machines, make every important decision, and it can describe its human review rule. The fourth is answered by describing the school's AI use levels and how teachers check that students are learning rather than just finishing tasks. For the fifth, the school names a contact person, explains how to request a child's records, and describes how to opt out where options exist, so families never have to guess whom to call.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, presenting the five questions and the answers a good school gives as a standard schools should meet. The only support offered is the claim that a school which cannot answer the questions clearly has more work to do, and that clear answers build trust.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here sit with the school, not the parent. A school that cannot answer the five questions clearly is told it has more work to do, which means the questions are a check on the school rather than a burden on families. The answers themselves carry conditions: agreements must limit how data is used, people must make every important decision, and opt outs exist only where options exist. The decisions that stay with people are the human review rule and the choice of which tools are approved, and a named contact person keeps concerns from being left to guesswork.
